rows: Expected service speed should be checked against the contract or provider information.
A suspected under-speed service should be diagnosed with the provider.
The right to exit can extend to financially, contractually or technically linked bundled products.
The code's 30-day remedy process does not apply in the same way to rolling monthly contracts.
Post-sale information should include estimates, policies affecting speed and remedies below guarantee.
Delayed service start or a missed engineer appointment can trigger automatic compensation.
Advertising rules use the average received by at least 50% of customers at the busiest time.
The coverage checker displays standard, superfast and ultrafast availability categories.
A personalised retail estimate or guarantee is not a measured speed for every parcel sharing a postcode.
A contract minimum guarantee cannot be substituted for the corrected Ofcom postcode coverage row.
Busy-time service estimates do not prove infrastructure availability at another premises.
The guide relies on provider-specific service information rather than a universal parcel dataset.
Consumer speed rights and estimates cannot replace strict inner-r2 archive validation.
No candidate is promoted from code-of-practice or contract-speed information alone.
The Ofcom social-tariff page was last updated on 22 June 2026.
Social tariffs are aimed at households receiving Universal Credit, Pension Credit or specified other benefits.
Ofcom reports current social-tariff prices from £10 to £24.
Ofcom says most listed tariffs offer speeds above 30 Mbit/s.
Setup cost should be zero or small and disclosed before signup.
Customers can switch to their provider's social tariff at any time without a fee.
Ofcom states the agreed social-tariff price should not rise mid-contract.
Social-tariff customers should not pay an early exit fee.
The benefit recipient generally needs to be the main person on the contract.
Some providers include additional qualifying benefits; eligibility is provider-specific.
The table lists a 30 Mbit/s 4th Utility social tariff in England.
BT Home Essentials includes a 36 Mbit/s UK offer.
BT Home Essentials includes a 67 Mbit/s UK offer.
Community Fibre Essential is listed at 35 Mbit/s for London.
Connect Fibre Essentials is listed at 150 Mbit/s in specified English counties.
G.Network Essential Fibre is listed at 50 Mbit/s in London.
Hyperoptic lists social-tariff tiers from 50 Mbit/s through 1 Gb/s in its service areas.
KCOM lists 30 and 50 Mbit/s social tariffs in Hull.
Quickline lists a 100 Mbit/s social tariff in Yorkshire and Lincolnshire.
Sky Broadband Basics is listed at 36 Mbit/s across the UK.
A tariff listing does not establish that the underlying network reaches a selected parcel.
Advertised package speed is not a measured parcel-level speed.
Geographic labels and 'where available' conditions prevent treating tariff presence as universal availability.
No candidate is promoted from price, eligibility or tariff speed alone.
The Spring 2026 Connected Nations update was published on 13 May 2026.
The report snapshots coverage and availability as of January 2026.
It is an interim update to Connected Nations 2025, whose base was July 2025.
Fixed broadband availability covers fixed-line and fixed-wireless-access networks.
The update separately reports full-fibre take-up.
Decent broadband is defined as at least 10 Mbit/s download and 1 Mbit/s upload.
Lower-priced Starlink plans in selected areas affect the affordable-decent-broadband count.
Mobile coverage uses MNO signal-strength predictions and is separate from fixed parcel coverage.
Full fibre is reported available to 24.9 million residential premises, 82% of 30.5 million homes.
Residential full-fibre availability increased by 1.2 million homes in six months.
Full-fibre take-up reached 12.4 million, an increase of 1.8 million.
Take-up is reported as 47% of premises with full-fibre access.
Gigabit-capable availability is reported at 27.1 million homes, or 89%.
The comparable July 2025 figure was 26.4 million homes, or 87%.
Only 4,000 premises are reported without affordable decent broadband.
39,000 premises lack decent broadband from fixed line or FWA, down from 44,000.
Gigabit and full-fibre coverage headline figures focus on residential properties.
Full-fibre take-up and no-decent-broadband counts cover residential and commercial premises combined.
The official fixed-broadband coverage and take-up archive is linked as a 32.2 MB ZIP.
Ofcom publishes an interactive report and summary tables alongside the update.
Ofcom says the collected data was used to update its broadband and mobile coverage checkers.
National availability percentages cannot be written as measured values for individual parcels.
No 3/4 promotion is allowed until exact corrected inner-r2 postcode rows pass strict validation.
